case_name: Alberta Union of Provincial Employees v. Edmonton Sun
text:
Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench

Alberta Union of Provincial Employees v. Edmonton Sun

Date: 1986-12-15

A. M. Zariski and C. Remmer, for plaintiffs.

K. G. Nielsen and M. F. Wesolowski, for defendants.

(Edmonton No. 8003-26736)

December 15, 1986.

[
1
]

McFadyen J
.:—

Introduction

[
2
]

The Alberta Union of Provincial Employees and 25 of its members who, at
the relevant time, were employed as correctional officers or guards at the Fort
Saskatchewan Correctional Centre bring this action in defamation arising from
the publication of three articles in the Edmonton Sun on 26th and 27th October
1978.

[
3
]

The action is brought against the proprietors of the Edmonton Sun, its
then publisher, William Bagshaw, a reporter, Allan Mayer, and a columnist, Eric
Denhoff. Mayer and Denhoff were both employees of the proprietors of the
newspaper at the relevant time.

[
4
]

The defendants admit the publication of the words in issue. Mayer admits
having written one of the articles complained of. Denhoff admits having written
the two columns which are the subject matter of this action.

I
ssues

[
5
]

The following issues have been raised:

1. The identification of the plaintiffs as the
persons referred to in the publication.

2. Were the articles or any of them defamatory of the
plaintiffs?

3. Do the statements complained of constitute
allegations of fact or comment?

4. Where facts are alleged, has truth been proved by
the defendants?

5. Whether the statements made are comments on a
matter of public interest and if so, have the defendants established the
defence of fair comment?

6. Has malice been established?

7. Had the plaintiffs given notice as required by the
provisions of s. 13 of the Defamation Act?

8. Assessment of damages including the award of
pre-judgment interest.

The Facts

[
6
]

On 24th October 1978 a hostage-taking incident occurred at the Fort
Saskatchewan Correctional Centre. This incident came to the attention of the
local media. Several photographers and reporters went to the correctional
centre to cover the story.

[
7
]

As members of the press arrived on the grounds of the correctional
centre, correctional centre staff asked them to wait in a house located near
the entrance. They waited there for some 15 to 30 minutes. After an ambulance
left the area, someone decided that the incident had terminated. Several people
left the house and went to the main building. Others followed. No one had
granted permission for this change of locale.

[
8
]

Thomas Walker, a freelance photographer who subsequently became an
employee of the Edmonton Sun, was following the group when he noticed several
correctional officers equipped with riot gear and batons. He took some
photographs of them, and then entered the building. Members of the media were
milling about in the foyer. As nothing interesting appeared to be happening,
Walker again went outside.

[
9
]

He saw Colin Shaw, the Edmonton Journal staff photographer, taking some
photographs of the guards. As Shaw approached the guards one of them advised
him that he was not permitted to take photos on the grounds. The guards then
escorted Shaw into the building.

[
10
]

Walker indicated that another guard advised him that he would have to
accompany him into the building. Two or three guards then escorted him into the
building. There he was advised that he would have to give up his film or wait
for the R.C.M.P. Walker then telephoned the Edmonton Sun office and spoke to an
assistant editor. Following this conversation he took out a new roll of film
and exposed it in the presence of the guard. He was then permitted to leave.

[
11
]

Although in one of the articles Walker is quoted as having said that a
guard grabbed him by the arm and forced him into the building, at trial he was
unable to recall any physical contact having occurred. He stated that he could
have been touched on the arm and shoulder. He testified that he had not been treated
roughly, but rather was escorted into the building after the guards left him
with the impression that he had no choice

in
the matter.

[
12
]

Colin Shaw confirmed the evidence of Walker about the waiting period in
the house. He indicated that as he entered the main building a receptionist was
distributing forms to be filled out by members of the press prior to entering
the secure area. Shaw noticed some guards moving about behind a glass security
door. He took some photographs of them through the glass. As he was doing so a
guard gestured to him to stop. He tried to open the security door and found
that it was locked.

[
13
]

He then went outside, where he started to take photographs of guards who
were in the process of putting away their gear. One of the guards told him that
he was not permitted to take their photographs and demanded that Shaw accompany
them into the building. Shaw confirmed that Walker was also escorted into the
building.

[
14
]

Ferguson, the assistant director, then demanded that Shaw give him the
film or it would be taken from him. Shaw does not recall a reference to the
R.CM.P. but concedes that this could have occurred.

[
15
]

After a heated exchange between the photographer and correctional centre
personnel, Shaw telephoned the Edmonton Journal office but was told to hang up
the phone in the middle of the conversation. While he was speaking on the phone
he believed that he overheard Ferguson advise one of the guards that the film
would be forcibly seized if Shaw failed to give it up voluntarily.

[
16
]

Shaw then removed the film from his camera and exposed it. He returned
to the Edmonton Journal office, where he reported the incident.

[
17
]

The only other witness who had a direct involvement in the incident
involving the photographers was Luke Rusk, one of the plaintiffs. Rusk
testified that as he approached the office of the assistant director, he saw a
photographer taking photographs through the glass. The photographer had also
shaken the security door. Ferguson told Rusk to ask the photographer to enter
his office. Rusk says that he spoke to the photographer and told him to come
in, that the assistant director wished to speak to him. This photographer has
been identified as Colin Shaw of the Edmonton Journal. Rusk denies having
touched Shaw or having made any threats to him. A conversation then ensued
between Shaw and Ferguson in which Ferguson demanded that he deliver up the
film.

[
18
]

Rusk recalls only the dealings with Shaw. He indicated that he had no
dealings with Walker. Rusk’s recollection does not coincide entirely with that
of the two photographers. The conflicts are of no particular relevance here.

[
19
]

Tim Thompson was one of the members of the tactical squad who were in
the process of removing their equipment inside the secure area when he saw a
photographer taking pictures through the security door. Thompson was not
involved with the photographers. He did see the photographers being escorted
into the administration area and over heard some of the conversation which
ensued. He confirmed that Downing advised the photographers that they would be
detained until the R.C.M.P. arrived if they did not give up the film.

[
20
]

Rossi Cameron, a reporter with the CBC, testified that she had asked for
and had received permission to do a report from the correctional centre grounds
with the building in the background. She was busy preparing her report when the
rest of the media rushed out to the main building. She and the CBC cameraman
followed at some distance behind them. As they approached the main building,
the photographer started filming guards who were in the process of stowing riot
gear into a van. One of the guards demanded the film and took a step towards
the photographer. Ms. Cameron stepped in front of him and advised the guard
that he could only get the film through proper channels. Following a verbal
exchange, Ms. Cameron and the photographer went to their vehicles. The guard
then indicated that he would call the R.C.M.P. and went to a telephone. The CBC
vehicle left the grounds unobstructed.

[
21
]

Crawshaw, a correctional officer who had been on perimeter duty, advised
that he had spoken to the CBC reporter on the grounds on two occasions. On the
first occasion he advised him that he could not take photographs unless he had
permission. On the second occasion Crawshaw was just going home and, having
learned that the photographer had no permission to take pictures, he asked him
to leave. Crawshaw then left the area. Crawshaw indicated he did not ask for
the film and did not threaten to call the R.C.M.P.

[
22
]

It is clear that Crawshaw was not the individual involved in the
incident with Ms. Cameron and the CBC photographer. I am satisfied that this
occurred subsequently to Crawshaw’s involvement with the photographer.

[
23
]

Rossi Cameron gave a report on the incident on the evening news.

[
24
]

On 25th October 1978 the Edmonton Journal published an editorial written
by Patrick O’Callaghan, then its publisher, as well as an interview with
O’Callaghan. O’Callaghan was very critical of the actions of correctional
centre staff in detaining the photographers and seizing the film. He used
phrases such as “jackboot mentality”, “goon mentality” and “this isn’t Nazi
Germany” in referring to the events.

[
25
]

No action has been commenced against the Edmonton Journal or Patrick
O’Callaghan.

The publications complained of

[
26
]

On 26th and 27th October 1978 three articles appeared in the Edmonton
Sun. The plaintiffs allege that these articles were defamatory of them.

[
27
]

An article written by Allan Mayer generally reported on the incident
involving the photographers. It contained quotes of statements made by Thomas
Walker, Patrick O’Callaghan and Bob King, the Assistant Deputy Minister of
Correctional Services, concerning the incident.

[
28
]

The plaintiffs claim that the following quotations from the Mayer
article were defamatory of them:

Sun photographer Tom Walker took Roy Farran’s advice Tuesday
and “kept his cool” while being manhandled by Fort Saskatchewan jail guards who
wanted to confiscate his film.

“One guard grabbed me by the arm and forced me
inside the main prison office,” Walker said.

“Another guard was yelling at the top of his lungs
at me. I don’t like getting bullied like that.”

Journal publisher J. P. O’Callaghan said his paper wouldn’t
tolerate “goon mentality”.

[
29
]

The plaintiffs claim that the following statements contained in an
article written by Eric Denhoff and published on the same page as the Mayer
article were defamatory of them:

And twice the wily boys from The Sun’s photography
department have outfoxed the former number one spy in Israel for the British
and his gang of bumbling yo-yos at the Fort Saskatchewan jail.

Or do what our photographers do — beat the yo-yos
at their own game . . .

The Journal writes very nasty things about Farran
saying it’s Nazi Germany. It Can’t Happen Here and “Jackboot mentality” . . .

The Sun doesn’t take these guys seriously — Farran
or his goons.

We simply treat them as they are — a joke.

Certainly, we get editorially upset about the
treatment, but let’s not give minor-leaguer Roy Farran and his gumshoes more
credibility than they deserve.

They haven’t got the brains to be Nazis, the
discipline to be jackboots or the mentality to philosophically endorse either
of the above.

[
30
]

In another article published on 27th October 1978 Denhoff made the
following statements which the plaintiffs claim defamed them:

Because she stood up to authority which had crossed
the line . . .

The goons asked her and her cameraman for the film
they had taken of the jail.

And the goon guard told her she had to turn it over
or they’d take it.

[
31
]

In this article Denhoff had been referring to an incident involving
Rossi Cameron, a CBC reporter who had refused to give up a film taken by a CBC
photographer.

Identification of the plaintiffs as the persons referred to

[
32
]

Each plaintiff has the onus of proving that he is the person or one of
the persons of whom or concerning whom the defamatory words were published.

[
33
]

Isaacs J. in
David Syme & Co. v. Canavan
(1918), 25 C.L.R.
234 at 238 (Aus. H.C.)
, referred to the following test:

The test of whether words that do not specifically name the
plaintiff refer to him or not is this: Are they such as reasonably in the
circumstances would lead persons acquainted with the plaintiff to believe that
he was the person referred to? That does not assume that those persons who read
the words know all the circumstances or all the relevant facts. But although
the plaintiff is not named in words, he may, nevertheless, be described so as
to be recognized; and whether that description takes the form of a word picture
of an individual or the form of a reference to a class of persons of which he
is or is believed to be a member, or any other form, if in the circumstances
the description is such that a person hearing or reading the alleged libel
would reasonably believe that the plaintiff was referred to, that is a
sufficient reference to him.

[
34
]

Group or class defamation was discussed by the House of Lords in
Knupffer
v. London Express Newspaper Ltd.,
[1944] A.C. 116, [1944] 1 All E.R. 495
.
Viscount Simon L.C. stated at p. 119:

Where the plaintiff is not named, the test which decides
whether the words used refer to him is the question whether the words are such
as would reasonably lead persons acquainted with the plaintiff to believe that
he was the person referred to. There are cases in which the language used in
reference to a limited class may be reasonably understood to refer to every
member of the class, in which case every member may have a cause of action.

At pp. 121-22 Lord Atkin stated as follows:

I venture to think that it is a mistake to lay down a rule
as to libel on a class, and then qualify it with exceptions. The only relevant
rule is that in order to be actionable the defamatory words must be understood
to be published of and concerning the plaintiff. It is irrelevant that the
words are published of two or more persons if they are proved to be published
of him, and it is irrelevant that the two or more persons are called by some
generic or class name.

[
35
]

I will first deal with the issue as to whether the plaintiff the Alberta
Union of Provincial Employees has identified itself as an entity that has been
defamed in these articles or any of them. The Alberta Union of Provincial
Employees has not satisfied me that any of the words published were defamatory
of it. While the Alberta Union of Provincial Employees may be well known as the
bargaining agent for correctional officers, nothing was published about it as a
union. No attack was made on its actions. Its association as the bargaining
agent for the guards is insufficient proof that it was defamed. The action by
the Alberta Union of Provincial Employees is dismissed.

[
36
]

Henceforth, when I refer to the plaintiffs I will be referring only to
the 25 individuals and not to the Alberta Union of Provincial Employees.

[
37
]

None of the plaintiffs was named in any of the articles. All were
employed at the time as correctional officers at the Fort Saskatchewan
Correctional Centre performing functions as guards. Some had been involved in a
hostage-taking incident as members of the tactical squad; others were on
stand-by in the event the incident escalated; others were performing their
usual duties at the correctional centre; others were absent on leave, on
training programs or performing other duties when the incident involving the
photographers occurred.

[
38
]

All testified that they believed that the articles, especially the first
Denhoff article, referred to them in a derogatory fashion. With the exception
of Tim Thompson, all of the plaintiffs testified that they had received
comments from friends, neighbours, relatives, acquaintances and strangers which
convinced them that these persons had read the articles and had identified them
with the articles either from personal knowledge or from the distinctive
uniform worn by the correctional officers employed at the Fort Saskatchewan
Correctional Centre.

[
39
]

The first two statements in the Mayer article refer specifically to the
actions of the guards who were involved in the incident with Walker. These were
specific individuals whose identities could be ascertained. None of the
plaintiffs played any part in the incident involving Walker. These portions of
the Mayer article contain no statement which refers to guards at the Fort
Saskatchewan Correctional Centre generally. They contain no statement which
would reasonably lead persons acquainted with each of the plaintiffs to believe
that he was the person referred to.

[
40
]

The quotation of words used by J. P. O’Callaghan is brief and makes no
reference to any particular individual or class of individuals. Again I am not
satisfied that the use of that quotation would lead a person who was acquainted
with the plaintiffs to believe that the person with whom he was acquainted was
the person referred to in the article.

[
41
]

The action against Allan Mayer is dismissed.

[
42
]

Similarly, the second Denhoff article refers only to the guard who was
participating in the incident involving Rossi Cameron. His identity is
ascertainable. None of the plaintiffs was involved in that incident. The words
complained of were not spoken of the plaintiffs and were not defamatory of
them.

[
43
]

To fully appreciate the effect of the Denhoff article published on 26th
October 1978 it is necessary to cite the comments complained of in their
context. This article commenced as follows:

Roy Farran, your spying days are over.

We’ve been playing your little game now for months,
Farran, and you are tired and beaten.

Twice, the solicitor-general of this province and
his jail guard boys at Fort Saskatchewan have tried to seize Sun film.

And twice the wily boys from The Sun’s
photography department have outfoxed the former number one spy in Israel for
the British and his gang of bumbling yo-yos at the Fort Saskatchewan jail.

[
44
]

Denhoff then discussed an incident involving a photographer named Alan
Scott and made certain critical comments of the Edmonton Journal’s coverage of
the incident in question.

[
45
]

He then continued:

Why didn’t The Journal photographer, reflecting the
freedom loving philosophy of that paper, stand up and say no?

Or do what our photographers do — beat the yo-yos at
their own game.

It doesn’t take much.

Roy Farran was once the hero of England for running
around Palestine telling the Jews they didn’t have a right to exist as a
nation.

He was Britain’s big intelligence guy.

And now his men have been outfoxed by a couple of
photographers.

The Journal writes very nasty things about
Farran saying it’s Nazi Germany. It Can’t Happen Here and ‘‘Jackboot
mentality’’.

But what are they doing about it?

The Sun doesn’t take these guys seriously —
Farran or his goons.

We simply treat them as they are — a joke.

Certainly, we get editorially upset about the
treatment, but let’s not give minor-leaguer Roy Farran and his gumshoes more
credibility than they deserve.

They haven’t got the brains to be Nazis, the
discipline to be jackboots or the mentality to philosophically endorse either
of the above.

[
46
]

This article does not specifically limit the application of the
statements to guards who were actually involved in the incident. It contains
such general references as “his jail guard boys”, “his gang of bumbling yo-yos
at the Fort Saskatchewan jail”.

[
47
]

The references in the portion of the article commencing with the
paragraph: “Why didn’t The Journal photographer, reflecting the freedom loving
philosophy of that paper, stand up and say no?” to the end of the article, can
only be interpreted as applying generally to all guards employed at the Fort
Saskatchewan Correctional Centre.

[
48
]

Denhoff testified that he intended to refer only to the Solicitor
General and to those individuals who were involved in the incident. The
intention of the author is of no consequence on the issue of identification if
the words used by him include individuals he did not intend to include.

[
49
]

Here the ordinary meaning of the words taken in the context of the whole
article includes all guards employed at the Fort Saskatchewan Correctional
Centre. The author made no effort to limit his remarks to specific individuals
or to the incident itself. I am satisfied that the ordinary, sensible reader
would reasonably believe that comments were made generally of guards employed
at the Fort Saskatchewan Correctional Centre. A reader who either knew one of
the plaintiffs and was aware that he performed such duties at the Fort
Saskatchewan Correctional Centre or who identified one of the plaintiffs by the
distinctive uniform which he wore would be of the opinion that this article
referred to that individual.

[
50
]

The group (approximately 200 individuals) is not so large as to make it
improbable that any ordinary reader would identify the plaintiffs as being
referred to in the statements. Nor are the claims of such a generalized or exaggerated
nature that no individual could reasonably identify them with the plaintiffs.

Is the 26th October 1978 Denhoff article defamatory of the
plaintiffs?

[
51
]

There is no precise definition as to what constitutes a defamatory
statement. Linden in Canadian Tort Law, 3rd ed. (1982), states at p. 676:

The classic definition, that was most widely used
until recently, declares that libel is that “which is calculated to injure the
reputation of another by exposing him to hatred, contempt or ridicule” to which
there is sometimes added that the words must cause a person to be “shunned or
avoided”. This definition, however, is now viewed as too narrow . . .

More recently, a formulation of the test has been expressed
to the effect that defamation “tends to lower a person in the estimation of
right-thinking members of society generally”. A variation of this latter test
is offered by Professor Fleming who contends that defamatory words “lower a
person in the estimation of his fellow men by making them think less of him’’.
Not very different than this is the requirement that the plaintiff has
“suffered in social reputation and in the opportunities of receiving respectful
consideration from the world”. One of the best tests yet devised is this:

“A communication is defamatory if it tends so to
harm the reputation of another as to lower him in the estimation of the
community or to deter third persons from associating or dealing with him.”

[
52
]

The article in question refers to the plaintiffs as a “gang of bumbling
yo-yos . . . goons . . . a joke” and finally ends with the statement: “They
haven’t got the brains to be Nazis, the discipline to be jackboots or the
mentality to philosophically endorse either of the above.”

[
53
]

The term “goons” connotes a lack of intelligence, incompetence and a
tendency towards brutality. The terms “yo-yos”, “bumbling yo-yos”, “a joke”
suggest stupidity or a lack of intelligence, a lack of competence and
discretion in the performance of one’s duties. The final statement again
indicates stupidity, incompetence, lack of discipline and discretion.

[
54
]

I have no doubt that all of these statements are defamatory of the
plaintiffs; that these statements exposed the plaintiffs to contempt and
ridicule; and that these statements lowered the plaintiffs in the estimation of
the communities in which they lived.

Are the words a statement of fact or a comment?

[
55
]

The defendants rely on the defence of fair comment. Before the
defendants can succeed in this defence, they must convince me that the words
are comment and not a statement of fact (see
Jones v. Skelton,
[1963] 1
W.L.R. 1362 at 1379, [1963] 3 All E.R. 952 (P.C.)
, cited with approval by
Ritchie J. in
Cherneskey v.

Armadale Publishers Ltd.,
1978 CanLII 20 (SCC)
, [1979] 1
S.C.R. 1067, [1978] 6 W.W.R. 618, 7 C.C.L.T. 69, 90 D.L.R. (3d) 321, 24 N.R.
271 [Sask.]). In Gatley on Libel and Slander, 8th ed. (1981), para. 699, the
following statement is made by the author:

Whether a statement is one of fact or is a comment
is a matter of interpretation in the light of all the circumstances known to
those to whom the words are published, in particular the context in which the
words appear. If in the light of those circumstances a reasonable member of the
public would understand the words as the expression of an opinion on facts, or
as an inference drawn from facts, the words will be held to be comment.

And in para. 701:

If a defamatory allegation is to be defended as
fair comment it must be recognisable by the ordinary reasonable man as comment
and not as a statement of fact.

In para. 704 the authors of the text state as follows:

So, too, if the defendant has failed to distinguish
clearly in what he has published between the facts on which he is commenting
and the comments he wishes to make on these facts, those to whom the words are
published may regard the comments either as statements of fact or as founded
upon unrevealed information in the possession of the publisher; in such
circumstances the publication may stand in the same position as any ordinary
allegation of fact.

In para. 705:

“. . . Any matter, therefore, which does not indicate with a
reasonable clearness that it purports to be comment, and not statement of fact,
cannot be protected by the plea of fair comment.”

In para. 706:

Nonetheless, it is clear that a comment can consist
of an inference of fact; that is, an author can assert, as his comment on facts
stated or referred to in what he publishes, some other fact the existence of
which he infers or deduces from those facts.

[
56
]

In Duncan and Neill on Defamation (1983), the learned authors state as
follows in para. 12.02:

The main principles relating to the defence of fair
comment may be stated as follows — . . .

(c) the comment, though it can consist of or include
inferences of fact, must be recognisable as comment.

[
57
]

In his evidence before me Denhoff indicated that he intended to make a
comment on the incident at the Fort Saskatchewan Correctional Centre, on the
actions of the Journal photographer and on the Journal coverage of the
incident.

[
58
]

While some portions of this article in fact achieved this objective,
other portions, however, take the form of a statement of fact. While the first
of the statements might be reasonably said to be an inference which was being
drawn by the author, from the fact that Walker and another Sun photographer
were able to substitute unexposed film when requested to produce film that they
had taken, the statements at the conclusion of the article purport to be and
can reasonably be viewed only as statements of fact. I particularly refer to
the portion of the article commencing with the words, “The Sun doesn’t take
these guys seriously — Farran or his goons.”

[
59
]

Clearly, no effort has been made to establish the truth of these
statements.

The defence of fair comment

[
60
]

The next issue is whether the defence of fair comment has been
established, even assuming that all statements complained of are comments.
Denhoff indicated that he had been hired as a political columnist. He viewed
his role as one of questioning authority and the action of the state. David
Bailey, now the editor in chief of the Edmonton Sun, also testified. He
indicated that the Denhoff article was published as Denhoff s commentary on the
incident in question. He confirmed that Denhoff had been hired as a columnist
whose role was to write articles making comments on various topics. Denhoff had
no responsibility as a reporter of the news. Bailey indicated that the Sun
would publish a column although it might not agree with the opinions expressed.

[
61
]

Denhoff stated that he honestly held the opinions stated by him. He also
indicated that he intended to refer only to the Solicitor General, the
administrative staff and the guards who were actually involved in the incident
and to express an opinion on an event and the people involved. In respect of
these individuals, he intended to portray an image of incompetence, of
bumbling; a lack of sophistication and a lack of intelligence. He intended to
use ridicule as a tool for the expression of his opinion.

[
62
]

Denhoff says that he did not intend to refer to any correctional centre
staff other than those individuals involved. He asserts no honest opinion or
belief that correctional centre staff generally lacked intelligence,
discipline, discretion or that they have a tendency towards brutality. Denhoff
further stated that he intended to comment only on the conduct of the
individuals in question and to draw inferences from that conduct. He did not
intend to ridicule the individuals as human beings or as individuals in
society.

[
63
]

Unfortunately, what may well have been intended to be a comment on the
behaviour of certain individuals involved in a specific incident turned out to
be a vitriolic attack on the intelligence, competence and tendency towards
violence not only of the individuals involved in the incident but also of other
individuals who performed functions of guards at the Fort Saskatchewan
Correctional Centre.

[
64
]

The defence of fair comment has been the subject of a great deal of
comment by the judiciary and by legal writers. I do not intend to cite
extensively from these opinions.

[
65
]

Martland J. in
Cherneskey v.

Armadale Publishers Ltd.
,
supra,
at pp. 324-25 stated as follows:

The reason for the existence of the defence of fair
comment in a suit for defamation, and the nature of that defence, are stated in

Salmond on Torts,
17th ed. (1977), p. 180, as follows:

“A fair comment on a matter which is of public
interest or is submitted to public criticism is not actionable. This right is
one of the aspects of the fundamental principle of freedom of expression, and
the courts are zealous to preserve it unimpaired. It must not be whittled down
by legal refinements. The jury are the guardians of the freedom of public
comment as well as of private character. It is only on the strongest grounds
that a court will set aside a verdict for a defendant when fair comment is
pleaded.

“Comment or criticism must be carefully
distinguished from a statement of fact. The former is not actionable if it
relates to a matter which is of public interest; the latter is actionable, even
though the facts so stated would, if true, have possessed the greatest public
interest and importance. Comment or criticism is essentially a statement of
opinion as to the estimate to be formed of a man’s writings or actions. Being
therefore a mere matter of opinion, and so incapable of definite proof, he who
expresses it is not called upon by the law to justify it as being true, but is
allowed to express it, even though others disagree with it, provided that it is
honest.”

Freedom to express an opinion on a matter of public
interest is protected, but such protection is afforded only when the opinion
represents the honest expression of the view of the person who expresses it.
This requirement is stated in the passage quoted above.
Galley on Libel and
Slander,
7th ed. (1974), p. 308, says: “Comment must be published honestly
in that it is the expression of the defendant’s real opinion.”

[
66
]

In this decision, Ritchie J. emphasized that the basis of the defence of
fair comment was the expression of an honestly held belief or opinion. The
burden of proving such an opinion lies on the defendant. Ritchie J., giving the
judgment for the majority, stated as follows at p. 330:

Accordingly, as I agree with the trial Judge that
the words used are capable of being construed as tending to lower the plaintiff
in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally, a
prima
facie
cause of action arises, and in my view a plea of fair comment by way
of defence does not of itself have the effect of saddling the plaintiff with
the burden of proving that the comment was unfair. This plea constitutes a
vital part of the case for the defendants and in my view the burden of proving
each ingredient of the defence so pleaded should rest upon the party asserting it.
One of these ingredients is that the person writing the material complained of
must be shown to have had an honest belief in the opinions expressed and it
will be seen that, in my view, the same considerations apply to each publisher
of that material.

[
67
]

The issue is not whether the author has an honest belief in the opinion
he intended or wished to express, but whether he had an honest belief in the
opinion actually conveyed to the reasonable person, the ordinary, sensible
reader of his material, by the words he chose to use. Linden, in Canadian Tort
Law, stated as follows at p. 694:

Moreover, the intended meaning of the speaker is not
relevant. Rather, the test is what meaning would be attributed to the words by
a reasonable reader or listener.

And at p. 695:

Similarly, the defendant will not escape responsibility upon
proof that he did not intend to refer to the plaintiff. “The question is not so
much who was aimed at as who was hit”.

[
68
]

Denhoff says that he intended to criticize the conduct of the guards
involved. He intended to use ridicule as a tool for conveying his opinion that
by their actions, the detention of the photographers and the failure to detect
the switch of films, the guards demonstrated a certain lack of sophistication,
intelligence and a bumbling, “keystone cops” type of behaviour.

[
69
]

This was his honestly held belief, the expression of which would
undoubtedly be accorded the protection of the defence of fair comment.

[
70
]

Denhoff asserted no honestly held belief in the statement of fact or
opinion which he has actually conveyed. He asserted no honestly held belief in
the general incompetence, brutality, lack of discipline, lack of intelligence
of the guards employed at the Fort Saskatchewan Correctional Centre.

[
71
]

In this case I need not decide whether the comment, if limited to the
individuals involved, would have been protected by the defence of fair comment.
Had it been necessary to do so I would have been inclined to the view that the
comments in the latter part went far beyond criticism and descended into the
arena of personal abuse and invective, which is not protected.

[
72
]

It is my view that, even assuming that all of the statements are
comments and not statements of fact as I have earlier found, the defence of
fair comment would not be available because of the lack of proof of an honestly
held belief in the meaning conveyed to a reasonable reader.

Malice

[
73
]

In any event, whether this issue is decided on the question of a lack of
proof by the defendant of criteria necessary to establish the defence of fair comment,
being honest belief, or whether it is dealt with on the basis of proof of
malice, as suggested by Dickson J. in the
Cherneskey

case, is
irrelevant. The evidence of Denhoff makes it clear that he held no honest
belief in the opinion his words conveyed, although he may have had an honest
belief in what he hoped to convey. By the words chosen by him, he attacked the
competence, the intelligence, the tendency towards violence and brutality, the
discipline of all persons performing the functions of jail guards at the Fort
Saskatchewan Correctional Centre.

[
74
]

The defendant the Sun and its proprietors do not rely on the provisions
of s. 9(1) of the Defamation Act; it is clear that this provision would not be
applicable in that Denhoff was employed as a columnist by the proprietors of
the newspaper.

[
75
]

Neither the defence of justification nor the defence of fair comment has
been established.

Notice — S. 13 of the Defamation Act

[
76
]

The defendant claims that the individual plaintiffs have not given
notice as required by s. 13 of the Defamation Act, which provides:

13(1) No action lies unless the plaintiff has, within 3
months after the publication of the defamatory matter has come to his notice or
knowledge, given to the defendant, in the case of a daily newspaper, 7, and in
the case of any other newspaper or when the defamatory matter was broadcast, 14
days’ notice in writing of his intention to bring an action, specifying the
defamatory matter complained of.

(2) The notice shall be served in the same manner as a
statement of claim.

[
77
]

The notice served in this case identified the proposed plaintiffs as
follows:

Take Notice
that
an action by:—

(1) The Alberta Union of Provincial Employees,

(2) John Booth, Mike Poulter, Shiona Osgoode, Paul
Duteau, Lloyd Hodgins, Roy St. C. Whyte and Albert Heuft, in their capacities
as officers of, trustees for and representatives of those members of Division 3
(being Correctional Officers) . . .

[
78
]

Albert Heuft is the only one of the 25 individual plaintiffs who was
specifically named in the notice, and only as a trustee for and a
representative for members of Division 3. Other individuals named in the notice
are officers of the Alberta Union of Provincial Employees. The other individual
plaintiffs are mentioned only in the general description “members of Division 3
(being Correctional Officers)”.

[
79
]

The defendant says that for the notice to be valid the plaintiff must be
identified in the notice and that the notice served fails to make a sufficient
identification.

[
80
]

The most recent Alberta decision of the notice required under the
Defamation Act is the decision of O’Byrne J. in
Paletta v. Lethbridge Herald
Co.
(1977),
1977 CanLII 537 (AB SCTD)
, 2 Alta. L.R. (2d) 166, 2 A.R. 529 (T.D.).

[
81
]

O’Byrne J. stated as follows at p. 169:

There are two lines of cases. One is strict stating
that such statutory provisions are mandatory and imperative. The other line
deals with the issue on the basis of whether or not there has been substantial
compliance. I prefer this line. It tends to protect common law rights unless
they are clearly taken away. The rule of beneficial construction is applied.

[
82
]

I agree with these comments. In
Grossman v.

CFTO-TV Ltd.
(1982),

1982 CanLII 1768 (ON CA)
, 39 O.R. (2d) 498, 139 D.L.R. (3d) 618, Cory J.A., giving the judgment of the Ontario
Court of Appeal, stated the purpose of the requirement of a notice as follows
at pp. 621-22:

The section stands as a condition precedent to the
commencement of an action for libel. It constitutes an absolute bar. The
purpose of the notice is to call the attention of the publishers to the alleged
libellous matter. When it is received an investigation can be made, and if the
publisher deems it appropriate, a correction, a retraction or apology can be
published. In this way the publisher can avoid or reduce the damages payable
for the publication of a libellous statement.

The plaintiff, as well, may benefit from the
notice. A timely correction, retraction or apology can often constitute a
better remedy than damages.

At p. 625 Cory J.A. formulated the following tests:

An appropriate test to determine whether the notice
complaining of a television broadcast is adequate might be as follows: Does the
notice identify the plaintiff and fairly bring home to the publisher the matter
complained of?

In
Sentinel-Review Co. v Robinson,
1928 CanLII 9 (SCC)
, [1928] S.C.R. 258,
[1928] 3 D.L.R. 97 [Ont.], Duff J. stated as follows at pp. 262-63:

Nor can I agree that the notice was not sufficient.
The statute prescribes no form. The notice is sufficient, if the plaintiff’s
intention to sue is notified. The communication must, of course, indicate the
intending plaintiff with reasonable certainty. But that is accomplished when
words are used which are calculated to apprise the addressee of the identity of
the complainant. I have no doubt that the notice in question did in fact inform
the respondents that the complainants were the proprietors of the
Sentinel-Review.

[
83
]

While the plaintiffs herein were not referred to by name, the intent to
bring an action on behalf of members of Division 3 of the Alberta Union of
Provincial Employees, who were identified as correctional officers, was clearly
specified in the notice. The defamatory material was clearly identified. By
this notice the defendants were made aware of the intent of correctional
officers to sue for defamation. The defendants were not made aware of their
names but were made aware of the general category of plaintiffs who intended to
sue.

[
84
]

It is my view that this is substantial compliance with the provisions of
the Defamation Act. I am satisfied that notice as required by s. 13 of the
Defamation Act was served.

Damages

[
85
]

Counsel for the defendant submits that the damages ought to be lessened
by reason of the prior publication in the Edmonton Journal of several of the
defamatory expressions subsequently used by Denhoff in his article. He points
out that at the time the Journal had a much greater circulation than the Sun.

[
86
]

Section 15(2) of the Defamation Act provides for the mitigation of
damages in certain cases as follows:

(2) The defendant may also prove in mitigation of damages
that the plaintiff has already brought action for, or has recovered damages, or
has received or agreed to receive compensation in respect of defamation to the
same purport or effect as that for which the action is brought.

[
87
]

Miller A.C.J.Q.B. in
Snider v.

Calgary Herald
(1985),
1985 CanLII 1244 (AB QB)
, 41
Alta. L.R. (2d) 11, 34 C.C.L.T. 27, 65 A.R. 99, considered the effect of s.
15(2) and stated as follows at p. 120:

[122] It would be much clearer if the plaintiff had obtained
a judgment in the prior action, or even made a negotiated settlement, to take
this into account in mitigating the damages to be awarded in this case. Neither
counsel could direct me to any decisions which would assist in laying down
guidelines for apportioning damages between concurrent suits and the section
itself offers no assistance. How can one calculate the mitigating effect of the
other action which may never get to trial or settlement? While it may seem
unfair to place the entire burden of damage upon the party who lands in court
first, nevertheless such a result is certainly open under the Act for s. 15(2)
places the burden upon the defendant to prove the extent of the mitigation.
However, before dealing with mitigation under this section I suggest that it is
first necessary to try and assess what this section is designed to accomplish.

[123] Defamation laws are designed to protect an individual
against damages resulting from loss of reputation due to published falsehoods.
The extent of the publication frequently affects the amount of damages awarded.
It seems to me that s. 15(2) is designed to prevent duplication of damages when
the falsehoods are published in the same area or to the same audience. For
example, if two newspapers circulating largely in the Edmonton area published
the same falsehood about a person it could fairly be assumed that many of the
same persons read the defamatory material in each newspaper and formed the same
opinion of the person’s reputation. The damage to the injured party would
overlap in such a case and the monetary award should be adjusted in some fair
manner to take this into account.

[
88
]

In that case an action had also been commenced against the Edmonton Sun
but had not yet been tried. Miller A.C.J.Q.B., interpreting the provisions of
s. 15, found that these were intended to avoid to some extent a duplication of
damages.

[
89
]

Clearly, s. 15 does not apply in this case, as the plaintiffs have
established that they have never commenced an action against the Edmonton
Journal.

[
90
]

Nor is there a common law right to mitigation of damages arising from
the mere fact that a similar defamation has been published by someone else.

[
91
]

In
Assoc. Newspapers v. Dingle,
[1964] A.C. 371, [1962] 3 W.L.R.
229 [1962] 2 All E.R. 737 (H.L.)
, Lord Denning considered this issue at pp.
410-11:

At one time in our law it was permissible for a
defendant to prove, in mitigation of damages, that, previously to his
publication, there were reports and rumours in circulation to the same effect
as the libel. That has long since ceased to be allowed, and for a good reason.
Our English law does not love tale-bearers. If the report or rumour was true,
let him justify it. If it was not true, he ought not to have repeated it or
aided its circulation. He must answer for it just as if he had started it
himself. Newspapers in particular must not speak ill about people for the spice
it gives their readers. It does a newspaper no good to say that other
newspapers did the same. They must answer for the effect of their own
circulation without reference to the damage done by others. They may not even
refer to other newspapers in mitigation of damages.

[
92
]

Counsel for the defendant relies on Gatley on Libel and Slander at p.
586, which reads as follows:

1434. Defendant not original author.
The
fact that the defendant was not the original author of the libel or slander,
but only published it by way of repetition, is no defence. It is, however, a
somewhat less malicious act to repeat than to originate a defamatory statement.
So, the defendant in an action for slander can prove in mitigation of damages
that he said at the time that he heard the slanderous matter from a named
person. Similarly, in libel the defendant may prove in mitigation that he
derived his information from a named person, or that he copied the words from a
newspaper, and that it is clear on the face of them that such is the fact.

[
93
]

I need not attempt to resolve the difficulty which the apparent conflict
of authorities raises. Nor do I need to decide whether the statements in the
articles published in the Edmonton Journal were defamatory of any of the
plaintiffs. While certain expressions were used in the Journal articles, some
care was taken by O’Callaghan to direct his comments to the incident which had
occurred and not to the individuals involved.

[
94
]

In his column, Denhoff was not quoting statements made by O’Callaghan.
Denhoff borrowed certain expressions used by O’Callaghan and applied them
generally to guards employed at the Fort Saskatchewan Correctional Centre.
Denhoff added some phrases of his own invention. The result was a searing
attack on the intelligence and competence of guards at the Fort Saskatchewan
Correctional Centre. Even on the broadest interpretation of the statements in
Gatley, damages will not be mitigated merely on the basis that some words have
been previously used by someone else. Here the words were used in an entirely
new context, and for the first time were directed against the group which included
the plaintiffs.

[
95
]

The plaintiffs are entitled to substantial damages. The Denhoff article
contained statements attacking their competence and their intelligence. The
article caused embarrassment and mental anguish to the plaintiffs. Although
allegations of incompetence, brutality and lack of intelligence of guards
generally were not true, the allegations served to exacerbate prejudices held
by certain individuals in the community and affected social and community
activities of many of the plaintiffs and their families.

[
96
]

None of the plaintiffs claims any special damages.

[
97
]

With one exception, all plaintiffs stated that their lives were affected
by the defamatory publication to some extent. Some plaintiffs had to endure
derogatory comments from a few people over a short period of time. Others were
subjected to numerous comments from relatives, friends, acquaintances and
strangers occurring with declining frequency over a period of one to two years.
Some plaintiffs and their families had to limit or avoid social and community
activities because of comments they received. Some felt they were being shunned
or avoided in their communities or at social events. All were hurt, embarrassed
and upset by the comments which each plaintiff believed referred to him. The
lives of spouses and children and parents were affected. Some plaintiffs gave
evidence that their children were subjected to prolonged name calling in school
as a result of publication of this article. Some of the plaintiffs had to
endure unusual or extraordinary mental anguish because of their personal
circumstances.

[
98
]

Rather than detailing the effects of the publication of the defamatory
material on each of the plaintiffs, I intend to separate them into three
groups. In the first group, I will place those individuals whose families and
whose activities were minimally affected by the publication of the defamatory
articles. To these individuals, Albert Heuft, Leonard Zietarski, Robert Mark,
Vernon Arthur Lutness, Jack Crawshaw, Tim Laird Thompson, Paul Steven Kratko and
S. B. Koenen, I award damages of $1,500.

[
99
]

The second group of individuals is the group whose lives and whose
families were seriously affected. They were subjected to derogatory comments
over a prolonged period of time. They had to avoid social and community
activities because of the embarrassment caused. Comments were made to their
spouses and children causing them further embarrassment and mental anguish.
They felt they were being avoided or shunned when attempting to participate in
social or community affairs. To the individuals in this group I award damages
in the amount of $2,500. These individuals are as follows: J. Highet, Gene
Stewart, Joseph Ronald Roy, Bryan James Trusty, Don R. Westman, Albert Cumby,
Randy Burynuik, Gerry Warren, Bruce Colin McLellan, Mario Boivin, Stan Roberts,
George Lowe, Gordon De Korver and Peter Critchley.

[
100
]

Because of their personal circumstances certain individuals suffered
extraordinary mental anguish as a result of the publication of the defamatory
material. I here refer to Luke Rusk, whose daughter was terminally ill at the
time, and Terry Kosack, whose father had been a prisoner in the Dachau
concentration camp. I award damages of $3,500 to each of these individuals.

[
101
]

Counsel for the plaintiffs has informed me that Robert Hatfield is now
deceased. While the publication was defamatory of him, I cannot award any
damages.

[
102
]

Interest will be awarded on the damages in accordance with the Judgment
Interest Act at the rate of 4 per cent per annum commencing on 1st April 1984.

Judgment for individual
plaintiffs.
